# Principal Component Analysis (PCA)


**(Running example: data matrices)**  Least squares used the data matrix to predict a response. PCA uses the same matrix to find the orthogonal directions along which the observations vary most. The SVD answers both questions.


## Definitions and Preprocessing


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Data Centering
Data matrix $\bX \in \fR^{n\times p}$ ($n$ samples, $p$ features) must be **centered**:
$$
\begin{align}
X_{ij} \leftarrow X_{ij} - \bar{x}_j, \quad \bar{x}_j = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_{ij}.
\end{align}
$$
Throughout this section, $\bX$ is assumed centered.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Sample Covariance Matrix
The matrix $\bS = \frac{1}{n-1}\bX^T\bX \in \fR^{p\times p}$.

- **Diagonal:**  $S_{jj}$ is the variance of feature $j$.

- **Off-diagonal:**  $S_{ij}$ is the covariance between features $i$ and $j$.

- **Property:**  $\bS$ is symmetric positive semidefinite (SPSD).

:::


::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Exercise
**Derive.**

1. Show that centering makes each column of $\bX$ have mean zero.

1. Prove that the diagonal entries of $\bS$ are sample variances.

1. Prove that $\bS$ is symmetric positive semidefinite by computing $\bz^T\bS\bz$.

:::


## PCA via SVD


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Principal Directions and Scores
Let $\bX = \bU\bsigma\bV^T$ be the SVD of the centered data matrix.

- **Principal Directions (Loadings):**  Columns of $\bV$ (eigenvectors of $\bS$).

- **Principal Components (Scores):**  $\bZ = \bX\bV = \bU\bsigma$.

- **Variances:**  $\lambda_i = \text{Var}(\bz_i) = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1}$.

:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false collapse=true}
## Proof
Substituting the SVD $\bX = \bU\bsigma\bV^T$ into the sample covariance matrix $\bS$:
$$
\begin{align}
\bS &= \frac{1}{n-1} \bX^T\bX \\
    &= \frac{1}{n-1} \left( \bV\bsigma^T\bU^T \right) \left( \bU\bsigma\bV^T \right) \\
    &= \frac{1}{n-1} \bV \bsigma^T (\bU^T\bU) \bsigma \bV^T \\
    &= \bV \left( \frac{\bsigma^2}{n-1} \right) \bV^T.
\end{align}
$$
Because $\bV$ is orthogonal and $\frac{\bsigma^2}{n-1}$ is diagonal with non-negative entries $\frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1}$, this is the spectral decomposition of $\bS$. The columns $\bv_i$ are eigenvectors of $\bS$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_i = \sigma_i^2 / (n-1)$.
The principal component score matrix is
$$
\begin{align}
\bZ = \bX\bV = \left( \bU\bsigma\bV^T \right) \bV = \bU\bsigma (\bV^T\bV) = \bU\bsigma.
\end{align}
$$
The sample covariance matrix of the scores is
$$
\begin{align}
\bS_{\bZ} = \frac{1}{n-1} \bZ^T\bZ = \frac{1}{n-1} (\bsigma\bU^T)(\bU\bsigma) = \frac{\bsigma^2}{n-1} = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, ..., \lambda_p),
\end{align}
$$
confirming that distinct score columns $\bz_i, \bz_j$ have sample covariance zero for $i \neq j$.
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Remark
**(PCA stability)**  Forming $\bX^T\bX$ squares the 2-norm condition number: $\kappa_2(\bX^T\bX)=\kappa_2(\bX)^2$ when $\bX$ has full column rank. Compute the singular vectors directly from an SVD when small singular values or numerical rank matter.
:::


::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Exercise
**Derive.**

1. Starting from $\bX=\bU\bsigma\bV^T$, compute $\bS=(n-1)^{-1}\bX^T\bX$.

1. Show that the columns of $\bV$ are eigenvectors of $\bS$.

1. Show that the corresponding eigenvalues are $\lambda_i=\sigma_i^2/(n-1)$.

1. Compute the score matrix $\bZ=\bX\bV$ and prove that $\operatorname{Cov}(\bZ)$ is diagonal.

1. Use the referenced result to explain the stability warning above.

:::


## Variance and Dimensionality Reduction


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Proportion of Variance Explained (PVE)
For the first $k$ components:
$$
\begin{align}
\text{PVE}_k = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^p \sigma_i^2}.
\end{align}
$$
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Theorem: Optimal Approximation
The rank-$k$ matrix
$$
\begin{align}
\bX_k = \sum_{i=1}^k \sigma_i \bu_i \bv_i^T
\end{align}
$$
is the optimal $k$-dimensional linear approximation of the data in the Frobenius norm, by the Eckart--Young theorem.
:::


::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Exercise
**Derive.**

1. Use the referenced result to prove the referenced result.

1. Show that $\|\bX-\bX_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2$.

1. Show that $\text{PVE}_k=1-\|\bX-\bX_k\|_F^2/\|\bX\|_F^2$.

1. Explain why a PVE threshold is a modeling choice, not a theorem.

:::


## Implementation Details


::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Remark
**(Standardization)**  If features have different units, PCA will be dominated by large-scale features. Standardize by dividing each centered column by its standard deviation: $X_{ij} \leftarrow (X_{ij} - \bar{x}_j)/s_j$.
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Remark
**(Interpretation)**  Principal components are directions of large variance. A large loading identifies a direction of variation in the data matrix. It does not by itself explain why that variation occurs.
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Definition: Dual PCA for $p \gg n$
When the number of features greatly exceeds the number of samples, we may diagonalize the $n\times n$ Gram matrix $\mathbf{K}=\bX\bX^T$ instead of the $p\times p$ covariance matrix. For each nonzero singular value, the feature-space principal direction is recovered from $\bv_i=\bX^T\bu_i/\sigma_i$. Kernel PCA replaces this linear Gram matrix by a centered nonlinear kernel matrix.
:::


## Exercises


::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Exercise

1. **Compute.**  Center $\bX = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \\ -1 & -4 \end{pmatrix}$ and compute $\bS$. Find the PVE for $k=1$.

1. **Derive.**  Prove that PC scores $\bz_i, \bz_j$ are uncorrelated for $i \neq j$ using the referenced result.

1. **Compute.**  Load the Iris dataset. Plot the data in the basis of the first two PCs. Do species cluster?

1. **Check.**  Verify that the sum of variances $\sum \lambda_i$ equals the total variance $\text{Tr}(\bS)$.

:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Further reading
Jolliffe is a standard statistical reference for principal component analysis [@jolliffe2002]. The Golub--Kahan paper gives the bidiagonalization behind modern large-scale SVD calculations [@golubkahan1965].
:::
